In [[mathematics]], the '''Markov–Kakutani fixed-point theorem''', named after [[Andrey Markov, Jr.|Andrey Markov]] and [[Shizuo Kakutani]],  states that a commuting family of continuous [[affine transformation|affine self-mappings]] of a [[convex set|compact convex subset]] in a [[locally convex topological vector space]] has a common fixed point. This theorem is a key tool in one of the quickest proofs of amenability of abelian groups.

==Statement==
Let <math>X</math> be a locally convex topological vector space, with a compact convex subset <math>K</math>. 
Let <math>S</math> be a family of continuous mappings of <math>K</math> to itself which commute and are ''affine'', meaning that <math>T(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) = \lambda T(x) + (1-\lambda)T(y)</math> for all <math>\lambda</math> in <math>(0,1)</math> and <math>T</math> in <math>S</math>. Then the mappings in <math>S</math> share a fixed point.{{sfn | Conway | 1990 | pp=151–152}}

==Proof for a single affine self-mapping==

Let <math>T</math> be a continuous affine self-mapping of <math>K</math>.

For <math>x</math> in <math>K</math> define a [[Net (mathematics)|net]] <math>\{x(N)\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}</math> in  <math>K</math> by

:<math> x(N)={1\over N+1}\sum_{n=0}^N T^n(x). </math>

Since <math>K</math> is compact, there is a convergent subnet in <math>K</math>:

:<math> x(N_i)\rightarrow y. \,</math>

To prove that <math>y</math> is a fixed point, it suffices to show that <math>f(Ty) = f(y)</math> for every <math>f</math> in the dual of <math>X</math>. (The dual separates points by the [[Hahn-Banach theorem]]; this is where the assumption of local convexity is used.)

Since <math>K</math> is compact, <math>|f|</math> is bounded on <math>K</math> by a positive constant <math>M</math>. On the other hand

:<math> |f(Tx(N))-f(x(N))|={1\over N+1} |f(T^{N+1}x)-f(x)|\le {2M\over N+1}. </math>

Taking <math>N = N_i</math> and passing to the limit as <math>i</math> goes to infinity, it follows that

:<math> f(Ty) = f(y). \, </math>

Hence

:<math>Ty = y. \, </math>

==Proof of theorem==
The set of fixed points of a single affine mapping <math>T</math> is a non-empty compact convex set <math>K^T</math> by the result for a single mapping. The other mappings in the family <math>S</math> commute with <math>T</math> so leave <math>K^T</math> invariant. Applying the result for a single mapping successively, it follows that any finite subset of <math>S</math> has a non-empty fixed point set given as the intersection of the compact convex sets <math>K^T</math> as <math>T</math> ranges over the subset. From the [[finite intersection property|compactness]] of <math>K</math> it follows that the set

:<math> K^S=\{y\in K\mid Ty=y, \, T\in S\}=\bigcap_{T\in S} K^T \,</math>

is non-empty (and compact and convex).
